options: TS2741, because `Vec` is missing the `Point` brand
No error, because `Vec` has every member that `Point` requires
TS2322, because `Vec` does not declare `implements Point`
TS2352, because a class instance needs a cast to an interface
questions.explanation: TypeScript is structurally typed: a value is assignable to `Point` if it has compatible `x` and `y` members, whatever class created it. `implements` is an optional check on the class declaration, not a requirement for assignability. There is no nominal brand on interfaces, so no cast is needed.

A `const` binding can never be reassigned, so TypeScript keeps the literal type `"hi"`. A `let` binding may later hold another string, so its type is widened to `string`. Widening happens on the mutable declaration, not the constant one.

Properties of an object literal are mutable, so `kind` is widened to `string` even though `shape` is `const`. `as const` keeps the literal type `"circle"` (and makes the property `readonly`). Switching to `let` changes nothing about the property, `Object.assign` still infers `string`, and `String(...)` returns `string`.

The array literal `[1, "a"]` is inferred as `(string | number)[]`, so `T` becomes `string | number` and the return type is `string | number | undefined`. TypeScript does not pick only the first element's type, and an array literal passed to `T[]` is not inferred as a tuple. `unknown` would only appear if there were no inference candidates.

options: No error; `unknown` behaves like `any` for member access
TS2339: `Property 'toFixed' does not exist on type 'object'`
questions.explanation: `unknown` is the type-safe top type: anything can be assigned to it, but you cannot use it until you narrow it, so TS18046 is reported on `x.toFixed`. `any` would allow the call silently. TS7006 is about missing annotations, and `x` is explicitly annotated here.

options: It compiles, and `area("triangle")` returns `undefined` at run time
TS2322: `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'`
TS2322: `Type '"triangle"' is not assignable to type 'never'`
questions.explanation: After the two `case` branches, `s` is narrowed to the remaining member `"triangle"`, which cannot be assigned to `never`, so tsc reports TS2322 naming that literal. This is the exhaustiveness-check pattern. The error mentions the leftover literal, not `string`, and the `default` branch returns, so there is no missing-return error.

A user-defined type guard with return type `pet is Fish` narrows the argument to `Fish` when it returns true and removes `Fish` from the union when it returns false. So the `else` branch sees `Bird`. A plain `boolean` return type would leave `Fish | Bird` in both branches.

options: It narrows `v` for the rest of the scope after the call, and must throw to signal failure
It narrows `v` just within an `if` that tests its boolean return value
It makes tsc insert a run-time `typeof` check at each call site
It makes tsc verify that the body throws for each non-string value
questions.explanation: An assertion function (TypeScript 3.7+) returns `void`; if it returns normally, the asserted type holds for the code that follows the call, so failure must be signalled by throwing. A type guard returns a boolean and narrows only in the branch that tests it. tsc never inserts run-time checks, and it does not verify that the body actually throws for non-strings; an assertion function that fails to check simply lies to the type checker.

options: TS2339: `Property 'length' does not exist on type 'object'`
TS2367: this comparison appears to be unintentional
questions.explanation: In JavaScript `typeof null` is `"object"`, and TypeScript models that: the check keeps both `string[]` and `null`, so `x.length` reports TS18047. Arrays also report `"object"`, so the comparison is valid. Use `x !== null` or a truthiness check to remove `null`.

options: TS2300 on both pairs: duplicate identifiers `User` and `Account`
No errors; both pairs merge into one type each
TS2300 on `Account` only; the two `User` interfaces merge into one
TS2300 on `User` only; the two `Account` aliases intersect
questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging: the two `User` declarations combine into `{ name: string; age: number }`. A type alias is a single named type and cannot be reopened, so the second `Account` triggers TS2300 `Duplicate identifier 'Account'`. Aliases never merge or intersect implicitly.

options: TS2339: `toUpperCase` is not a member of every type in `string | number`
TS2345: a union cannot be passed where `string` methods are called
TS7006: the parameter needs an explicit `string` annotation
TS18048: `x` may be `undefined` inside the function
questions.explanation: On a union you can only access members that exist on every constituent. `number` has no `toUpperCase`, so tsc reports TS2339 on `string | number`. Narrow first, e.g. `typeof x === "string"`. The parameter is annotated and cannot be `undefined`, so the other errors do not apply.

questions.prompt:
What is the type of `Both["id"]`?

```ts
type Both = { id: string } & { id: number };
```
questions.explanation: An intersection requires a value to satisfy both object types, so `id` must be `string & number`, which has no values and reduces to `never`. A union would give `string | number`. Intersections do not let one side win; you only get a usable type when the property types overlap.

options: Both reject `.red.toUpperCase()`, since both have the declared type `Colors`
Both compile `.red.toUpperCase()`, because `satisfies` is a type assertion
questions.explanation: `satisfies` (TypeScript 4.9) checks the expression against `Colors` but keeps the expression's own inferred type, so `a.red` stays `string`. The annotation on `b` replaces the inferred type with `Colors`, so `b.red` is `string | [number, number, number]` and `toUpperCase` is TS2339. `satisfies` is a check, not an assertion like `as`.

A constraint (`extends`) tells the checker what every `T` is guaranteed to have, so `x.length` becomes valid and both `"abc"` and `[1, 2]` satisfy it. A default (`= ...`) is only used when nothing is inferred and gives no guarantee. `object` has no `length`, and it also rules out strings.

`K extends keyof T` limits `key` to `"name" | "age"` for `user`, so `"email"` is TS2345. The last call passes a different object whose keys include `email`, so it is valid. The return type `T[K]` also gives `string` for `name` and `number` for `age`.

A `const` type parameter (TypeScript 5.0) makes inference behave as if the argument were written with `as const`, so the array literal becomes the readonly tuple `readonly ["a", "b"]`. Without `const`, `T` would be `string[]`. Neither `("a" | "b")[]` nor a mutable `[string, string]` is what `as const` produces.

options: TS2345: `Argument of type '"c"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"a" | "b"'`
TS2344: `NoInfer` requires a concrete type, not a type parameter
questions.explanation: `NoInfer<T>` (TypeScript 5.4) blocks `fallback` from contributing an inference candidate, so `T` is inferred from `values` alone as `"a" | "b"`, and `"c"` is then rejected with TS2345. Without `NoInfer`, `"c"` would be added to `T` and the call would compile. It does not widen anything and works on type parameters.

A conditional type whose checked type is a naked type parameter distributes over unions, so `ToArray` is applied to `string` and `number` separately. Wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple turns distribution off, so `ToArrayND` sees the whole union at once. Distribution only depends on whether the checked type is a bare type parameter.

options: `A` is `true | false`; `B` is a compile error
questions.explanation: `infer U` declares a type variable that is filled in when the match succeeds, so for `boolean[]` it captures `boolean`. `number` is not an array, so the false branch `never` is used. A failed match is not an error, and `infer` without a constraint does not fall back to `unknown` when the branch is not taken.

`ReturnType<typeof loadUser>` is `Promise<{ id: number; name: string }>` because an `async` function returns a promise. `Awaited` unwraps promises recursively, giving the object type. Object literal properties are widened, so the literal types `1` and `"Ada"` are not kept.

options: TS2344: `fetchUser` does not satisfy the constraint of `ReturnType`
TS2749: `'fetchUser' refers to a value, but is being used as a type here`
questions.explanation: A function declaration creates a value, not a type, so naming it in a type position is TS2749 (tsc even suggests `typeof fetchUser`). The fix is `ReturnType<typeof fetchUser>`. The name does exist, so it is not TS2304, and the constraint check never runs because there is no type to check.

The `as` clause (TypeScript 4.1) remaps each key: `Capitalize<"name">` is `"Name"`, so the new key is `getName`, and the value type still uses the original key `K`. Without `as` the keys would stay `name` and `age`. `Capitalize` changes the first letter, and remapping over a finite key set does not produce an index signature.

questions.prompt:
How many members does the union `T` have?

```ts
type T = `${"top" | "bottom"}-${"left" | "center" | "right"}`;
```
questions.explanation: When a template literal type interpolates unions, TypeScript produces the cross product of all combinations: 2 x 3 = 6 strings, such as `"top-left"` and `"bottom-right"`. It does not pair members positionally (which would give 2 or 3) and does not add them (5).

`as const` makes `roles` a readonly tuple of literal types, `typeof roles` lifts that into a type, and indexing with `number` gives the union of all element types. Without `as const` the array would be `string[]` and `Role` would be `string`. Indexing by `number` gives element types, not the index type.

`typeof config` gives the object type `{ host: string; port: number }`, and `keyof` turns it into the union of its property names. `string | number` would be the value types (`(typeof config)[keyof typeof config]`). `keyof` only returns `string` for a type with a string index signature.

options: Neither emits code; both are replaced by their values at each use
`Dir` gets a reverse mapping (`Dir[0] === "Up"`), while `Color` maps names to values one way
`Color` gets a reverse mapping (`Color.RED === "Red"`), while `Dir` maps names to values one way
Both get reverse mappings, so `Dir[0]` and `Color["RED"]` return the member names
questions.explanation: Regular enums are real run-time objects. For numeric members tsc emits `Dir[Dir["Up"] = 0] = "Up"`, so the object maps both ways; string members are emitted as plain `Color["Red"] = "RED"` with no reverse entry. Inlining with no emitted object is what `const enum` does, not a regular enum.

options: A TS2475 error, because a `const enum` is not allowed in an expression
questions.explanation: A `const enum` exists only at compile time: tsc replaces each member access with its literal value (adding a comment) and emits no enum object, unless `preserveConstEnums` is set. TS2475 is reported only when the enum object itself is used, e.g. `Object.keys(Level)`; a member access is allowed. Because inlining needs the declaration's values, tools that compile one file at a time (`isolatedModules`) restrict ambient const enums.

options: Both are enforced by the JavaScript engine once compiled
`private` is enforced at run time; `#secret` is checked only by tsc
Both are erased by tsc, so neither is enforced at run time
`private` is checked only by tsc; `#secret` is enforced by the engine at run time
questions.explanation: TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time check that is erased, so `(a as any).secret` or `a["secret"]` reads the field at run time. `#secret` is a JavaScript private field (ES2022): the engine hides it, it does not appear in `Object.keys` or JSON, and outside access is a syntax error. tsc keeps `#` fields in its output (or downlevels them with WeakMaps for old targets).

options: It declares the fields `name` and `age` and assigns the arguments to them
It declares the parameters, and fields must be declared separately
It declares `age` as a field, but `name` stays a local parameter
It is a TS1187 error; modifiers belong on fields, not parameters
questions.explanation: These are parameter properties: an access modifier or `readonly` on a constructor parameter both declares a class property and emits `this.name = name` in the constructor. Every modified parameter becomes a field, including `private readonly name`. Parameter properties are a TypeScript-only feature (not erasable syntax), which is why they appear in the emitted JavaScript as assignments.

options: No error; `describe` makes the class concrete
TS2515: `Shape` does not implement the abstract member `area`
TS2511: `Cannot create an instance of an abstract class`
TS2564: the abstract property `area` has no initializer
questions.explanation: An `abstract` class cannot be instantiated directly (TS2511), even if it has some implemented methods. TS2515 is reported on a non-abstract subclass that fails to implement an abstract member, not on the abstract class itself. `area` is a method, so property-initialization errors do not apply.

options: No error; the implementation signature accepts `string | number`
No error; tsc picks the first overload and returns `string`
TS2394: the overloads are incompatible with the implementation
questions.explanation: Callers only see the overload signatures; the implementation signature is hidden. Neither overload accepts `string | number` on its own, so tsc reports TS2769. The overloads are compatible with the implementation, so TS2394 does not apply. The fix is to add a third overload `(x: string | number): string | number`.

questions.prompt:
Which line does `tsc --strict` reject?

```ts
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
const tmp = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };
const a: Point = tmp;                     // line A
const b: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };    // line B
const c: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 } as Point; // line C
```
questions.explanation: Excess property checking applies only to fresh object literals assigned directly to a typed target, so line B gets TS2353 (`'z' does not exist in type 'Point'`). Line A assigns a variable, which is ordinary structural assignability, and extra properties are fine. Line C uses a type assertion, which skips the excess property check.

`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `undefined` to every read through an index signature or array index, because the checker cannot prove the element exists. It is not part of `strict`, so without the flag `first` is just `string`. The annotation `string[]` drops the literal, and out-of-range reads give `undefined`, not `null`.

questions.prompt:
With `strict` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled, which assignment is an error?

```ts
interface Prefs { theme?: string }
```
questions.explanation: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes `theme?: string` mean "may be missing" but not "may be present with the value `undefined`", so `{ theme: undefined }` is TS2375. Omitting the property is still fine. To allow an explicit `undefined`, write `theme?: string | undefined`. The flag is not included in `strict`.

`useUnknownInCatchVariables` is part of `strict` since TypeScript 4.4, so catch variables are `unknown` and must be narrowed (for example with `err instanceof Error`). Without that flag they are `any`. TypeScript has no checked exceptions, so it cannot infer `Error` or `SyntaxError` from the `try` body.

options: No error; `import type` only affects the emitted JavaScript
TS1361: `'User' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'`
TS2693: `'User' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here`
questions.explanation: `import type` imports only the type side of a binding and is always erased, so using `User` as a constructor is TS1361. You can still write `let u: User`. TS2693 is the error for names that are only types to begin with, like an interface, whereas `User` is a class that was imported type-only.

options: tsc removes the import because `Config` is used just as a type
tsc keeps it as `import { Config } from "./config"`
tsc reports TS1484: a type must be imported with `import type`
tsc rewrites it to `import "./config"` to keep side effects
questions.explanation: Under `verbatimModuleSyntax`, imports without a `type` modifier are emitted exactly as written, so importing a type-only name that way would leave a broken import at run time. tsc therefore reports TS1484 (`'Config' is a type and must be imported using a type-only import`). Removing type-only imports silently is what happened before this flag; it is not what happens with it.

questions.prompt:
Under `strict`, `import fmt from "tiny-fmt"` fails with TS7016 (`Could not find a declaration file for module 'tiny-fmt'`). Which fix gives the import real, non-`any` types?

```ts
import fmt from "tiny-fmt";
```
options: Add the shorthand `declare module "tiny-fmt";` to a `.d.ts` file
Put a `// @ts-ignore` comment directly above the import
questions.explanation: A module declaration with a body describes the module's exports, so `fmt` gets the declared signature (installing a matching `@types/tiny-fmt` package from DefinitelyTyped would do the same). The shorthand `declare module "tiny-fmt";` silences the error but types every import as `any`, as does `@ts-ignore`. `skipLibCheck` only skips checking existing `.d.ts` files.

questions.prompt:
With `module` and `moduleResolution` set to `nodenext`, in a package with `"type": "module"`, what does tsc report for this import in `main.ts`?

```ts
import { add } from "./math";
```
options: TS2835: relative imports need explicit file extensions; it suggests `./math.js`
TS2307: `./math` is not found, and it suggests `./math.ts`
TS2691: an import path may not end with a `.ts` extension
questions.explanation: Node's ESM loader does not guess extensions, and `nodenext` models that, so an extensionless relative import is TS2835. You write the extension of the emitted file, `./math.js`, and tsc maps it back to `math.ts`. `moduleResolution: "bundler"` would accept the extensionless path, because bundlers do add extensions.

questions.prompt:
With `"target": "ES2017"` and no explicit `lib`, what does tsc report for this line?

```ts
const last = [1, 2, 3].at(-1);
```
options: No error; tsc adds a polyfill for `Array.prototype.at`
No error; `target` affects syntax alone, so the newest built-in types are available
TS2550: `Property 'at' does not exist`, with a hint to change `lib` to es2022 or later
TS1005: `at` is reserved syntax that the ES2017 parser rejects
questions.explanation: When `lib` is not set, its default follows `target`, so only ES2017 built-in declarations are loaded and `at` (ES2022) is TS2550. tsc never polyfills APIs; `target` controls which syntax gets downleveled and `lib` controls which built-in types exist. Setting `lib` to include `es2022` makes it type-check, but the runtime must still provide `at`.

Function parameters are checked contravariantly under `strictFunctionTypes`: a handler that needs a `Dog` cannot stand in for one that may receive any `Animal`, so `onAnimal = onDog` is TS2322. The reverse is safe, return types are covariant, and arrays are (unsoundly) covariant, so the other three compile.

questions.prompt: With `"strict": true` and default options, tsc refuses to emit JavaScript for a file that has type errors.
questions.explanation: Type checking and emit are independent: by default tsc reports the errors and still writes the JavaScript. Only `noEmitOnError: true` suppresses output when there are errors. `strict` changes which errors are reported, not whether output is produced.

questions.prompt: An `interface` declaration produces no JavaScript at all in tsc's output.
questions.explanation: Interfaces, type aliases and other type-only constructs are erased completely, which is why you cannot test `x instanceof SomeInterface` at run time. By contrast, `class` and regular `enum` declarations do produce JavaScript because they are values.

questions.prompt: Under `strictFunctionTypes`, parameters of members declared with method syntax (`m(x: Dog): void`) are still compared bivariantly.
questions.explanation: `strictFunctionTypes` applies only to function-type syntax such as `m: (x: Dog) => void`; method and constructor declarations are deliberately exempt so that types like `Array<T>` stay covariant. So assigning `{ m(x: Dog): void }` to `{ m(x: Animal): void }` compiles, while the same with property syntax is TS2322.

questions.prompt: Assigning a `Dog[]` to a variable of type `Animal[]` compiles under `strict`, even though pushing a `Cat` through that variable then breaks the original array's type.
questions.explanation: Mutable arrays are treated covariantly for convenience, which is a known unsoundness: tsc accepts `const animals: Animal[] = dogs; animals.push(cat);`. Typing the target as `readonly Animal[]` removes the risk because it has no `push`.

questions.prompt: Setting `"strict": true` also enables `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`.
questions.explanation: `strict` enables `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitThis`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` and `alwaysStrict`. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`) must be turned on separately, so `arr[0]` on a `string[]` is plain `string` under `strict` alone.

questions.prompt: A `type` alias can be declared a second time with the same name to add more properties, just like an interface.
questions.explanation: Only interfaces (and namespaces, enums and some others) take part in declaration merging. A second `type` with the same name is TS2300 `Duplicate identifier`. To extend an alias, create a new one with an intersection such as `type B = A & { extra: string }`.

questions.prompt: A value of type `unknown` can be assigned to a variable of type `string` without narrowing or a cast.
questions.explanation: `unknown` accepts every value, but it is assignable only to `unknown` and `any`. Assigning it to `string` is TS2322 until you narrow it (for example with `typeof v === "string"`) or assert. That restriction is what makes `unknown` safer than `any`.

questions.prompt: A value of type `never` can be assigned to a variable of any other type.
questions.explanation: `never` is the bottom type: it has no values, so it is a subtype of every type and assignable to all of them. That is why a function that always throws can be used where any return type is expected. The reverse is not true: nothing except `never` (and `any` is not an exception here) is assignable to `never`.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.5 and later, `[1, undefined, 2].filter(x => x !== undefined)` is inferred as `number[]` without writing an explicit type predicate.
questions.explanation: TypeScript 5.5 added inferred type predicates: an arrow function like `x => x !== undefined` is inferred as `(x) => x is number`, and `filter` uses that overload. Before 5.5 the result stayed `(number | undefined)[]` unless you wrote `(x): x is number => ...` yourself.

questions.prompt: By default, tsc replaces each `const enum` member access with its literal value and emits no enum object.
questions.explanation: That inlining is the purpose of `const enum`: `Level.High` becomes `2 /* Level.High */`. The `preserveConstEnums` option keeps the object in the output as well, and `isolatedModules` restricts using ambient const enums because a single-file transpiler cannot see their values.

questions.prompt: Excess property checking also applies when you assign an existing variable (not a fresh object literal) to a narrower object type.
questions.explanation: Only fresh object literals are checked for unknown properties, because extra keys there are almost always typos. A variable holding `{ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }` is assignable to `{ x: number; y: number }` by normal structural rules, so the extra `z` passes silently.

questions.prompt: `expr satisfies T` changes the inferred type of `expr` to `T`.
questions.explanation: `satisfies` (TypeScript 4.9) only checks that the expression is assignable to `T` and leaves the inferred type unchanged, keeping specific literal and property types. A type annotation or `as T` is what replaces the type with `T`.

questions.prompt: A function declared with return type `never` may simply reach the end of its body, implicitly returning `undefined`.
questions.explanation: A `never` return type means the function never completes normally: it must throw or loop forever. If the end of the body is reachable, tsc reports TS2534 `A function returning 'never' cannot have a reachable end point`. A function that returns nothing useful should be typed `void` instead.

questions.prompt: Without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, reading `scores.anyKey` on a `Record<string, number>` is typed as plain `number`, even if the key is missing at run time.
questions.explanation: A string index signature promises a value for every key, so reads are typed `number` and a missing key silently yields `undefined` at run time. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` changes such reads to `number | undefined`, forcing a check.

questions.prompt: TypeScript's `private` modifier stops other code from reading the property at run time.
questions.explanation: `private` is checked by tsc and then erased; the emitted JavaScript has an ordinary property that anything can read, and even TypeScript allows `obj["secret"]` bracket access. Use a JavaScript `#private` field when you need run-time privacy.

questions.prompt:
Which checks narrow `x` from `string[] | null` to `string[]` inside the `if` block?

```ts
declare const x: string[] | null;
```
questions.explanation: Truthiness removes `null`, `x !== null` removes it directly, and `Array.isArray` is declared as a type guard (`arg is any[]`), so all three leave `string[]`. `typeof null` is `"object"`, so that check keeps `null`. The `undefined` check removes nothing because `undefined` was never in the union.

questions.prompt: Which of these produce no JavaScript output at all when compiled by tsc?
questions.explanation: Interfaces, type aliases and `import type` exist only for the type checker and are erased. A regular `enum` compiles to an object, and a class with a parameter property compiles to a class whose constructor assigns `this.x = x`. These two are TypeScript-specific syntax that generates code, which is why Node's type stripping rejects them.

questions.prompt: Which of these flags does `"strict": true` turn on in TypeScript 5.6?
questions.explanation: The `strict` family is `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `noImplicitThis`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (since 4.4) and `alwaysStrict`. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` are stricter still and must be enabled explicitly, because they would break a lot of existing code.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript 5.x's `lib.es5.d.ts`, which utility types are defined as conditional types?
questions.explanation: `Exclude` is `T extends U ? never : T`, and `ReturnType` and `Parameters` use `infer` inside a conditional type. `Partial` is a mapped type. `NonNullable` used to be a conditional type but has been `T & {}` since TypeScript 4.8, which lets the intersection simplify better.

questions.prompt: Which statements about interfaces and type aliases are correct in TypeScript 5.x?
options: Interfaces support declaration merging; type aliases do not
A type alias can name a union such as `string | number`
A class can `implements` an object-shaped type alias
An interface cannot `extends` a type alias
A type alias cannot take type parameters
questions.explanation: Repeated interface declarations merge, while a repeated alias is TS2300. Aliases can name any type, including unions, primitives and tuples, which interfaces cannot. A class may implement, and an interface may extend, any object-shaped alias, and aliases can be generic (`type Box<T> = { value: T }`).

Anything is assignable to `unknown`, and `any` is assignable to everything (that is what makes it unsafe). `{}` means "any non-nullish value", so a primitive like `0` fits. `unknown` cannot be assigned to `string` without narrowing (TS2322), and nothing is assignable to `never`.

questions.prompt:
Which statements about `as const` are correct?

```ts
const settings = { mode: "dark", sizes: [12, 14] } as const;
```
options: At run time the object is frozen, so assignments throw
Nested values stay mutable; only top-level properties become readonly
questions.explanation: `as const` applies recursively to the literal: strings and numbers keep their literal types, arrays become readonly tuples and every property becomes `readonly`, so the assignment is TS2540. It is purely a compile-time assertion and is erased, so nothing is frozen at run time; use `Object.freeze` for that.

questions.prompt: Which types resolve to exactly `string`?
questions.explanation: `Extract` keeps the union members assignable to `string`, `Exclude` removes `number`, and `NonNullable` (`T & {}`) strips `null` and `undefined`, so all three give `string`. `keyof string` is the union of `number` and the names of `String.prototype` members. The return type keeps `void`, so it is `string | void`.

questions.prompt: Which of these does TypeScript use to narrow a union type?
questions.explanation: `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in` and equality checks on a discriminant property are all recognised by control-flow analysis. `Object.keys(x).length` is an ordinary expression with a `number` result; tsc does not derive any type information from it, so `x` keeps its declared type.

questions.prompt:
Which of these strings are assignable to the type `Id`?

```ts
type Id = `user-${number}`;
```
questions.explanation: A `${number}` placeholder accepts any string that parses as a number, including decimals, so `"user-42"` and `"user-3.5"` fit. An empty or non-numeric suffix is TS2322, and the literal prefix is case-sensitive, so `"User-7"` fails too.

questions.prompt: Which of these compiler options change the JavaScript that tsc emits (not just which errors it reports)?
questions.explanation: `target` decides which syntax is downleveled (for example `class` fields or `?.`), and `module` decides the module format (ESM `import` or CommonJS `require`). `lib` only selects built-in type declarations, and the two checking flags only add or remove errors; none of them alter the output. Note that `strict` itself does affect emit, because it includes `alwaysStrict`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about abstract classes in TypeScript are correct?
options: They can contain fully implemented methods
`new` on an abstract class is a compile error
A non-abstract subclass must implement every abstract member
They are erased like interfaces and emit no JavaScript
questions.explanation: Abstract classes can mix implemented and `abstract` members and can have constructors that subclasses call with `super()`. Instantiating one is TS2511, and a concrete subclass that skips an abstract member gets TS2515. Unlike interfaces they are real classes in the output; only the `abstract` keyword and abstract members are erased.

questions.prompt: Which statements about function overloads in TypeScript are correct?
options: Callers cannot call the implementation signature directly
Each overload must be compatible with the implementation signature
The emitted JavaScript contains one function body
tsc tries the overloads in declaration order and picks the first match
At run time the engine dispatches to the overload matching the argument types
questions.explanation: Overload signatures are type-only: the output has a single function, and JavaScript has no type-based dispatch, so the implementation must inspect its arguments itself. tsc resolves a call against the overloads top to bottom, which is why more specific overloads go first. An overload the implementation cannot satisfy is TS2394, and the implementation signature is invisible to callers.

questions.prompt: Given `type T = { readonly a?: number; b?: string }`, which of these produce exactly `{ a: number; b: string }` (no `readonly`, no optional)?
questions.explanation: `-readonly` and `-?` remove the two modifiers, so applying both (in one mapped type or in two steps) gives the plain type. `Required<T>` removes `?` but keeps `readonly a`. Removing only `readonly` leaves the properties optional, and `Partial<Readonly<T>>` adds modifiers rather than removing them.

questions.prompt: Given `interface Dog extends Animal { bark(): void }`, which assignments compile under `--strict`?
options: A `(a: Animal) => void` to a `(d: Dog) => void` variable
A `(d: Dog) => void` to a `(a: Animal) => void` variable
A `() => Dog` to a `() => Animal` variable
questions.explanation: Parameters are contravariant under `strictFunctionTypes`, so a function that accepts any `Animal` can be used where a `Dog` handler is expected, but not the reverse (TS2322). Return types are covariant. Arrays are treated covariantly, which allows `Dog[]` to `Animal[]`. A readonly array cannot become a mutable one, and `Animal` is not a `Dog` either.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `any` are correct under `--strict`?
options: A property read on an `any` value is also `any`
An `any` value can be assigned to a `number` variable without a cast
`strict` reports an error whenever you write `any` explicitly
Calling an `any` value as a function compiles
`any` and `unknown` allow the same operations without narrowing
questions.explanation: `any` switches off checking: member access, calls and assignment to other types all compile, and the `any`-ness spreads through property reads. `noImplicitAny` only flags implicit `any`; an explicit annotation is allowed (linters can ban it). `unknown` is the opposite: it allows almost nothing until narrowed.

questions.prompt: Your app imports the untyped npm package `left-pad-x`. Which of these are legitimate ways to get type declarations for it?
options: Install `@types/left-pad-x` from DefinitelyTyped if it exists
Use the package's own bundled `.d.ts`, found via `types` or `exports` in its `package.json`
Write a local `.d.ts` file with `declare module "left-pad-x" { ... }`
Enable `allowJs`, which makes tsc read the package's JavaScript inside `node_modules`
Set `skipLibCheck: false` so tsc generates the missing types
questions.explanation: Types come either from the package itself (`types` or `exports` conditions in `package.json`), from a DefinitelyTyped `@types/*` package, or from your own ambient module declaration. `allowJs` does not reach into `node_modules` by default (`maxNodeModuleJsDepth` is 0), and `skipLibCheck` only controls whether existing declaration files are checked.

questions.prompt: Which statements about type-only imports and erasure are correct?
options: `import type { A } from "./a"` is removed from the emitted JavaScript
`import { type A, b } from "./a"` keeps the import but drops `A` from it
A type imported with `import type` can still be used in annotations
`import type` makes tsc check the imported value at run time
Interfaces can be checked at run time with `instanceof`
questions.explanation: `import type` is erased entirely, and an inline `type` modifier drops just that specifier while keeping the import for the remaining values. Either way the name is still usable in type positions. Types have no run-time representation, so tsc never emits checks for them, and `instanceof` with an interface is TS2693 because only values can appear on its right side.

questions.prompt: Order these types from narrowest (fewest possible values) to widest.
questions.explanation: `never` has no values and `unknown` contains every value, so they are the bottom and top of the type lattice. In between, each type is assignable to the next: the literal `"a"` fits in `"a" | "b"`, which fits in `string`. None of the reverse assignments compile.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of the TypeScript compiler (tsc) from first to last.
options: Scanner turns source text into tokens
Parser builds the abstract syntax tree
Binder creates symbols and connects declarations
Emitter writes JavaScript and declaration files
questions.explanation: tsc scans characters into tokens, parses them into an AST, binds names to symbols, type-checks using those symbols, and finally emits output. Emit runs after checking but does not depend on it succeeding, which is why errors and output can coexist unless `noEmitOnError` is set.

questions.prompt: Each type below is assignable to the next. Order them from most specific to least specific.
questions.explanation: Structural subtyping: narrowing a property to a literal gives a subtype, and removing properties gives a supertype (more objects match). `{}` accepts any non-nullish value, and `unknown` also includes `null` and `undefined`. No step can be reversed without a TS2322 error.

Control-flow analysis removes each case that has already returned: after the `null` check `null` is gone, after the boolean check `boolean` is gone, and after the number check only `string` remains at the final `return`.

questions.prompt: With `moduleResolution: "node10"`, tsc resolves `import _ from "lodash"` from `/app/src/main.ts`. Order the locations it tries, from first to last (stopping at the first hit).
questions.explanation: Like Node's CommonJS algorithm, tsc looks in the nearest `node_modules` first, and in each one it tries the package itself (its `package.json` `types`, then `index.d.ts`) before the matching `@types` package. Only then does it walk up to the parent directory's `node_modules` and repeat. `--traceResolution` prints this sequence.

In a derived class, `this` is only available after `super()`. tsc emits the parameter-property assignments first, then the field initializers, and then the remaining constructor statements, all right after the `super()` call.

questions.prompt: Given `type T = { a: 1; b: 2; c: 3; d: 4 }`, order these types from fewest to most properties.
questions.explanation: `Pick` keeps one key, `Omit` of two keys leaves two, `Omit` of one key leaves three, `Partial` keeps all four (only making them optional), and the intersection adds a fifth property `e`.

questions.prompt: Each type is assignable to the next one but not the other way round. Order them from most specific to least specific.
questions.explanation: A mutable tuple of literals is a `string[]`; any mutable array is assignable to its readonly form; a readonly array is iterable; and everything fits in `unknown`. The reverse directions fail: a readonly array has no `push`, an `Iterable` has no indexes or `length`, and `string[]` does not have a fixed length.

questions.prompt: Order these TypeScript features by the release that introduced them, from oldest to newest.
questions.explanation: `unknown` arrived in TypeScript 3.0, assertion functions in 3.7, template literal types in 4.1, `satisfies` in 4.9 and `const` type parameters in 5.0.

questions.prompt: The TypeScript `const input = JSON.parse(raw) as number; console.log(input + 1);` compiles cleanly. tsc erases the assertion and emits the JavaScript below. What does it log?
questions.explanation: A type assertion is erased and does no conversion or check, so `input` is still the string `"1"` at run time. `"1" + 1` concatenates to `"11"`. Validate parsed data at run time (for example with a schema) instead of asserting its type.

questions.prompt: tsc compiles `enum Dir { Up, Down }` to the JavaScript below. What does it log?
questions.explanation: The inner assignment `Dir["Up"] = 0` evaluates to `0`, which is then used as a key mapping back to `"Up"`. So the object holds both name-to-number and number-to-name entries, and `Object.keys` lists the integer keys first. This is why iterating a numeric enum's keys yields twice as many entries as members.

questions.prompt: tsc compiles `enum Color { Red = "RED" }` to the JavaScript below. What does it log?
questions.explanation: String enum members get no reverse mapping, so the object only maps `Red` to `"RED"` and looking up `"RED"` gives `undefined`. Only numeric members are emitted with the `E[E["k"] = v] = "k"` pattern.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript, `Account` declared `private secret: string` and `Vault` uses a JavaScript `#secret` field. Below is the emitted JavaScript (target ES2022). What does it log?
questions.explanation: `private` is erased, leaving an ordinary public property that can be read and is serialized by `JSON.stringify`. A `#secret` field is a separate private slot: `v.secret` is a different, nonexistent property (`undefined`), and private fields are not own enumerable properties, so the JSON is `{}`.

questions.prompt: In TypeScript, `user` was typed with `as { age: number }`, so `user.age + 1` compiled. Below is the emitted JavaScript. What does it log?
questions.explanation: The type annotation disappears at compile time, so nothing checks that `age` is really a number. The JSON contains the string `"42"`, so `+ 1` concatenates to `"421"`. Types describe what you expect, not what arrives over the wire.

questions.prompt: tsc reports TS2540 (`Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property`) for the TypeScript version of this code, which used `as const`. Because `noEmitOnError` is off by default, it still emits the JavaScript below. What does it log?
questions.explanation: `as const` is a compile-time assertion; it is erased and does not call `Object.freeze`, so the assignment succeeds at run time and the object is not frozen. tsc reports the error but writes output anyway unless `noEmitOnError` is enabled.
